scenes.title: Splitting a force into components

beats.text: A rope pulling at an angle both drags the box forwards and lifts it. Splitting the force into two components at right angles shows each job on its own.
The force is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle: horizontal side adjacent to theta, vertical side opposite.
Adjacent equals hypotenuse times cos theta, so the horizontal component is F cos theta.
Opposite equals hypotenuse times sine theta, so the vertical component is F sine theta.
Check the extremes. Theta zero: cos zero is one, all drag, no lift. Theta ninety: all lift, no drag.

scenes.title: Two or more forces

beats.text: With several forces, resolve each one, then add the horizontal parts and the vertical parts.
Horizontally: R x equals F one cos theta one, plus F two cos theta two.
Vertically: R y equals F one sine theta one, plus F two sine theta two.
These totals are the resultant’s components, so Pythagoras gives its size.
And tan theta equals R y over R x gives its direction.

scenes.title: Picture the whole journey

beats.text: Consider a box resting on a smooth, horizontal floor. A rope tied to it slopes upwards at sixty degrees to the floor.
Someone pulls the rope steadily. The box starts to move and picks up speed along the floor... faster every second.
Notice: the box slides but never lifts off. The rope pulls forwards and upwards at once. How heavy is the box, and how hard does the floor push up on it?

scenes.title: The whole question

beats.text: The rope pulls with a force of sixteen newtons, at sixty degrees above the horizontal.
The box accelerates along the floor at two metres per second squared.
Take g as ten metres per second squared. The floor is smooth, so there is no friction.
The box stays on the floor, so no vertical acceleration. The rope is light.
Find the mass m, and the normal reaction R from the floor.

scenes.title: Resolve the pull

beats.text: Three forces act: the pull, the weight m g down, the reaction R up. Only the pull is angled, so we split it.
Horizontal component: H equals F cos theta.
Sixteen cos sixty degrees. Cos sixty is a half, so H is eight newtons.
Vertical component: V equals F sine theta.
Sixteen sine sixty: eight root three, about thirteen point nine newtons. H and V now replace the sixteen newtons.

scenes.title: Apply Newton’s second law

beats.text: Newton’s second law: resultant force equals mass times acceleration, one direction at a time.
Horizontally, the floor is smooth, so H is the only horizontal force.
Substitute: eight equals m times two.
So the mass is four kilograms.
Vertically there is no acceleration, so up balances down: R plus V equals m g.
Substitute: R plus eight root three equals four times ten.
So R equals forty minus eight root three.
About twenty-six point one newtons.
The weight is forty newtons; the floor pushes up with only twenty-six. The rope carries the rest.
If the rope were horizontal, V would be zero and R would equal the full weight, forty newtons.

scenes.title: Weight on a slope

beats.text: Now the box rests on a smooth slope at angle theta, nothing pulling it. Weight acts straight down; the reaction is perpendicular to the slope. With axes along and across the slope, the weight is the force we split.
Why is the angle between weight and perpendicular also theta? Turn the horizontal and the slope by ninety degrees: they become the vertical and the perpendicular, same angle between them.
Down the slope, the component of weight is m g sine theta.
Into the slope, it is m g cos theta.
Conditions: smooth slope, box stays on it, nothing else presses into it. Then perpendicular forces balance: R equals m g cos theta.
Along the slope, m g sine theta equals m a, so it accelerates down at g sine theta, whatever its mass.
